title: Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
disposition_detail: Issue 1 (whether Metro Atlanta Presbytery violated a BCO procedural requirement by dissolving Grace North Atlanta Church without its consent): No. Issue 2 (whether the presbytery clearly erred in a matter of discretion and judgment by dissolving the church): No. Complaint denied.
first_summary: TE Tolivar Wills complained after Metro Atlanta Presbytery dissolved Grace North Atlanta Church without the congregation’s consent and then denied his re-filed complaint. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that BCO 13-9.f permits a presbytery to dissolve a church and that BCO 40-6 does not require formal process for dissolution. It also found no clear error in the presbytery’s discretionary decision. The dissolution therefore stood, though the SJC cautioned that dissolution must be justified and reviewable.
summary: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: Case 2016-14, Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery, SJC decision on complaint, 45th GA (2017), decided March 3, 2017. RE Donahoe drafted the proposed decision; the panel approved it, and the full SJC amended and adopted it by roll call vote (20 concur, 2 recused, 2 absent). Source: cases/ga45_2017__2016-14.md, lines 13–15, 234–240; printed pp. 543–554. No separate merits opinion appears.
evidence_notes.dispute: Wills challenged Metro Atlanta Presbytery’s June 29, 2015 dissolution of Grace North Atlanta Church without the church’s consent, after the presbytery denied his re-filed complaint on September 20, 2016. The SJC framed two issues: whether MAP violated a BCO procedural requirement by dissolving without consent, and whether MAP clearly erred in its discretionary judgment to dissolve. Lines 111–119, 127–129, 149–161, 197–203.
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: The SJC answered both issues No and denied the complaint. Issue 1: BCO 13-9.f grants presbyteries power to dissolve churches; BCO 40-6 does not mention dissolution and imposes no formal process here, so there was no constitutional violation. Issue 2: dissolution is discretionary; under BCO 39-3.3 the SJC reverses only for clear error, and the record did not show clear error. Lines 163–169, 171–232.
evidence_notes.qualifications: The SJC cautioned that dissolution still must be prudent, reasonable, and supported by sufficient justification; had MAP dissolved without sufficient justification, the SJC said it would have found clear error. The decision also states that dissolution procedures remain reviewable even though no procedure is constitutionally mandated. Lines 223–232. The source also contains proposed OMSJC amendments and an officer election, which were not adjudicated in this complaint. Lines 242–300.
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: The decision recounts prior Case 2015-12 (Wills v. MAP), in which the SJC ruled the earlier complaint administratively out of order and directed filing with MAP within 30 days; it also quotes the prior Case 2015-03 mootness ruling and references Hardie Appeal 2015-08. Lines 31, 127–143. Those incorporated results are used only as procedural history; no material incorporated result is missing.
